transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2026-03-04 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Daniel Kim (CTO - Aquila), Priya Rao (Head of ML - Aquila), Liam O'Connor (Infra Lead - Aquila)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Aquila is evaluating Redwood for payment-notification and fraud-detection features. Primary concern is predictable p95 latency under 50ms for short prompts and streaming token throughput for longer contexts. They're weighing Hosted for quick rollout, Dedicated for guaranteed throughput, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for compliance. Requested a benchmark using their sample workload (mix of short intents + longer multi-turn chat), plus SOC2/KMS docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, this is Sofia our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Daniel Kim: Good, thanks. Quick, on time. We wanted to talk through latency/throughput requirements and see where Redwood fits.
[00:11] Sofia Martinez: Nice to meet you all. Could you kick off with your current stack and what SLOs you're trying to hit?
[00:16] Priya Rao: Sure, we run a mix of inference on AWS EKS with some self-hosted endpoints for older models. For the new payments recommender + fraud alerts we need low p95, ideally <120ms for short prompts (like 30-60 token prompts), and for streaming chat-like flows maybe p95 of 500-700ms for first token but sustained token/sec matters — we want at least 20-30 tokens/sec steady for longer responses.
[00:38] Liam O'Connor: Concurrency-wise, bursts hit about 200 concurrent requests during peak windows, average concurrency is more like 30. A lot of requests are short. Also want to make sure streaming works end-to-end over our mobile clients.
[00:52] Jordan Lee: That's super helpful. When you say p95 <120ms for short prompts, is that including network hop or just server-side generation?
[00:58] Priya Rao: Ideally end-to-end from API invocation to first token delivered to the client. But we can separate network overhead — our internal infra adds ~20-30ms on average.
[01:08] Sofia Martinez: Okay, so server-side target would be closer to 90-100ms p95. For hosted we publish typical p95 ranges for our verified models — for small turn prompts we often see p95 around 60-120ms on optimized kernels with batching off or very small batches. For dedicated, with pinned capacity and reserved GPU pools, you get tighter p95 and more consistent tail latencies.
[01:28] Daniel Kim: Can you explain how Redwood handles streaming versus non-streaming? We saw some jitter in a POC with another vendor.
[01:34] Sofia Martinez: Sure. We support chunked streaming where tokens are flushed as they're generated; the runtime prioritizes low-latency first-token by using continuous batching and prioritization. For longer sequences we keep an eye on KV cache and streaming flush intervals. That said, network chunking from client SDK can introduce variability.
[01:52] Priya Rao: What's your approach to batching? We want low latency for short prompts but efficiency for longer ones to control cost.
[01:57] Sofia Martinez: Good question. We do dynamic batching: the runtime groups requests with similar sequence length and urgency. For latency-sensitive routes you can set max_batch_size=1 or enable a micro-batching policy that waits only a few ms. We also have prefix/KV caching to speed up repeated contexts (helps a lot for multi-turn payment flows where the prompt shares a lot of history).
[02:17] Liam O'Connor: Do you support model quantization and what's the perf hit? We're curious about 4-bit quantized variants to reduce cost but not lose too much latency predictability.
[02:24] Sofia Martinez: Yes, we support quantized model variants; performance depends on GPU and kernel selection. For 4-bit we often see similar p95 for int8/4-bit on newer Ampere/Blackwell hardware for generation throughput, but it's model-dependent. Our runtime picks optimized kernels per model to avoid latency spikes.
[02:40] Daniel Kim: For a benchmark we'll want to measure p95, p99, and tokens/sec at different concurrencies — can Redwood run that or do you need us to run locally?
[02:48] Jordan Lee: We can run the benchmark if you give us representative traffic and samples. Typical plan: 1) share traffic profile (percent short vs long, tokens distribution), 2) Redwood runs hosted and dedicated tests measuring p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec (both cold and warmed KV cache), 3) we share raw logs and a spreadsheet with results.
[03:05] Priya Rao: How long does the benchmark usually take? We need to align with our compliance window.
[03:09] Sofia Martinez: End-to-end usually 2-3 days including setup and a couple of runs at different concurrencies. If you want Private (VPC) tests we can do a remote runner that lives in your VPC; that adds a day for network setup.
[03:20] Liam O'Connor: On the dedicated side, how do you guarantee throughput? We need reserved GPU pools and autoscaling but no noisy neighbor.
[03:27] Jordan Lee: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools plus configurable autoscaling policies and isolation. You can pin model versions and we also have rules to route traffic to fallback variants if capacity is constrained. SLAs are attached to committed throughput and we provide token-level cost breakdowns.
[03:40] Daniel Kim: Security — we need SOC2, SSO, KMS/HSM, audit logs, and data residency in EU for some customers.
[03:47] Jordan Lee: We have SOC2 Type II, support SSO via SAML/Okta, KMS integrations, and audit logs with retention options. For data residency we can operate in EU regions or do Private VPC/on-prem deployments. We'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs after this call.
[04:02] Priya Rao: One more — how does Redwood handle model rollouts and fallback? If a new model regresses, can we automatically fallback to a previous variant?
[04:09] Sofia Martinez: Yes, rollout policies support canary and A/B and automatic fallback to pinned variants if latency or quality regressions are detected. We tie evaluations to prompt sets so you can monitor quality.
[04:20] Jordan Lee: Back to numbers — can you give a concrete example of your expected load for the benchmark? p95 target, percent of streaming vs short-turn?
[04:26] Liam O'Connor: Sure — typical peak: 200 concurrent requests, 85% short intents (30-60 tokens), 15% streaming multi-turn sessions with average 300 tokens per response. p95 target: <=120ms end-to-end for short intents, for streaming first-token p95 <=600ms, sustained streaming >=25 tokens/sec. We'll send a CSV with timestamps and sample payloads.
[04:46] Sofia Martinez: That profile is ideal. For hosted we can run a throughput test at 50, 100, and 200 concurrency and report p95/p99 and tokens/sec under warmed cache and cold start. For dedicated we'll run the same with pinned capacity — you'll see much flatter tails.
[05:01] Daniel Kim: How do you measure tokens/sec — aggregate across GPUs or per-request? We care about per-request sustained token/sec for streaming latency.
[05:08] Sofia Martinez: We report both: overall cluster tokens/sec and per-request tokens/sec distributions. For streaming SLOs we look at first-token latency and then token inter-arrival times for sustained throughput.
[05:18] Priya Rao: Any gotchas with mobile streaming — chunk sizes, SDK buffer sizes? We've seen clients buffer a lot which makes it look like a server issue.
[05:24] Sofia Martinez: Yeah, client-side buffering can mask real server latency. We'll run a test using your mobile SDK where possible; otherwise we emulate typical mobile behavior. We recommend small chunk sizes and immediate flush on the first token for low-first-token SLOs.
[05:36] Jordan Lee: Quick cost talk — do you have a target CPI/token or are you optimizing for latency regardless of cost?
[05:42] Daniel Kim: We're trying to balance both. For fraud alerts cost is more flexible if latency is guaranteed; for recommendation widgets cost matters more. So we'll want a breakdown of cost-per-1k tokens for hosted vs dedicated, and an estimate of savings with quantized models.
[05:58] Jordan Lee: We will include cost estimates and a quantization comparison in the pricing doc.
[06:02] Priya Rao: For the benchmark data — can you anonymize logs and only take perf metrics? We can't share raw PII.
[06:07] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We can accept synthetic or anonymized payloads; our benchmark tooling doesn't need PII and we can run with redacted inputs.
[06:14] Liam O'Connor: Network — if we do private deployment, can you integrate with our HSM? We need keys on-prem for certain flows.
[06:21] Sofia Martinez: We support KMS/HSM integrations; on private you can bring your own key material with HSM. We'll loop in the security team if you move forward.
[06:30] Daniel Kim: Competitors. We did a short eval of Mistral and OpenAI endpoints; Mistral on-prem had nice throughput but tail latencies were inconsistent. OpenAI had lower operational work but cost at scale was a concern.
[06:44] Jordan Lee: Good context. Redwood tries to hit a middle ground: high throughput with production economics and transparent tradeoffs.
[06:50] Sofia Martinez: Practical question — do you want Redwood to run hosted benchmarks first or set up a dedicated trial?
[06:55] Priya Rao: Let's start with hosted to move quickly, then dedicated if results look good, and Private for regulated customers.
[07:03] Jordan Lee: Great. We'll run hosted and dedicated. We'll need: sample traffic CSV, a list of representative prompts, and your SLOs which you already described. Any other constraints?
[07:12] Liam O'Connor: One more — can you simulate KV-cache warm states? A lot of our multi-turn flows benefit from warmed caches.
[07:17] Sofia Martinez: Yes we'll do cold and warmed runs; we'll document cache hit rates and how that affects per-token cost.
[07:24] Daniel Kim: Timeline: Can you do initial hosted benchmark next week?
[07:27] Jordan Lee: Yes, if we get the traffic profile by Friday we can run tests early next week and share results mid-next-week.
[07:34] Priya Rao: Sounds good. Also please include streaming metrics broken down by token position (first token vs steady-state).
[07:40] Jordan Lee: Noted.
[07:42] Sofia Martinez: I'll also ask for sample mobile SDK logs if you can share — helps us emulate client behavior.
[07:48] Daniel Kim: We'll send over the CSV and sample payloads, anonymized.
[07:51] Jordan Lee: Awesome. Quick recap of next steps before we close?
[07:55] Priya Rao: Send pricing and security docs; Redwood to run hosted + dedicated benchmarks; Aquila to provide traffic profiles and sample payloads.
[08:02] Jordan Lee: Perfect. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark runs and the pricing doc.
[08:08] Daniel Kim: Thanks, bye.
